correctness.rationale: Exact product-Legendre orthogonality isolates the squarefree highest-degree kernel and controls its remainder uniformly in L2 by O_m(d^((m-1)/2)). Normalized symmetric polynomials of a bounded triangular array converge via Lindeberg, empirical quadratic variation, vanishing higher power sums and Newton identities to the probabilists Hermite polynomial. Uniform second moments make absolute-value expectations converge; a subsequence compactness argument yields a uniform local statement. Endpoint corners attain the sharp asymptotic, and strict monotonicity of the profile gives the exact near-maximizer criterion. The quadratic coefficient is an analytically evaluated Gaussian absolute moment. Executed finite checks confirm formula/normalization but are not the infinite proof.

evidence: 2014 De Marchi–Sommariva–Vianello gives √(max K(a,a)) upper bounds for hyperinterpolation; at cube corners the leading coefficient for fixed m and d growing is 3^(m/2)/sqrt(m!), strictly larger than the sharp coefficient here for m>=1.

2014 Wang–Wang–Wang abstract states Chebyshev-weighted hyperinterpolation with asymptotic order as polynomial degree increases, which does not determine uniform-weight Legendre orthogonal-projection norm for fixed degree as ambient dimension grows.

Defant et al. (2022) develops projection constants in trigonometric groups, complex analytic polynomial spaces and discrete Boolean cubes; the 2026 representation-theoretic results address homogeneous group spaces such as tori, spheres and unitary groups.
broader_coverage.reasoning: A generic Christoffel norm upper bound is not an equality claim and has a strictly larger leading constant. The identified broader projection-constant studies do not dominate the real continuous cube with uniform product Legendre measure, and the Chebyshev hyperinterpolation literature uses different weights/discretized operators and another asymptotic variable.

evidence: Trefethen (2016), theorem 4.2, proves exponential convergence-rate comparisons for total, Euclidean and maximal polynomial degree under analyticity; it does not give an L∞ operator norm of a fixed-degree Legendre projector.
Szili–Vértesi (2009) is described as triangular partial sums of multivariate Fourier series, a different trigonometric space and growing-frequency problem.

De Marchi–Sommariva–Vianello (2014), product Jacobi section, gives orthonormal basis and Christoffel estimates compatible with but weaker than the sharp absolute integral; a separate Gaussian-chaos and uniformity argument is necessary.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Neither approximation rates nor trigonometric triangular Fourier-sum norm orders can imply the claimed continuous Legendre norm. The closest diagonal-kernel bound gives only the growth exponent and a nonsharp coefficient; there is no implication to exact asymptotic coefficient, local profile, or if-and-only-if near-maximizer condition. Prior one-degree affine or discrete Johnson results likewise do not cover all fixed degrees at least two on the uniform continuous cube.

Published results on the quadratic Johnson idempotent and on the degree-two Hamming scheme are discrete association-scheme projections, not the Legendre integral projector on a continuous cube.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The theorem can be rephrased as a sharp Lebesgue constant, an L1 reproducing-kernel norm, or worst-case C(Q)-to-C(Q) error amplification. The identified prior statements cover either only the L2 diagonal norm, a different probability measure, a different discrete polynomial basis, or approximation error rather than this dimension-normalized sharp L1 kernel and mean-square evaluation profile. Matching Hermite-type limits in discrete schemes do not imply the continuous Legendre coefficient or uniform localization.

value.rationale: For a canonical fixed-degree multivariate least-squares projector, computes the previously unestablished sharp leading dimension-growth constant, its full uniform local dependence on the evaluation geometry, and the necessary/sufficient near-corner rigidity condition. Its coefficient is strictly smaller than the generic Christoffel-diagonal upper bound and provides a sharp worst-case approximation stability benchmark in the high-dimensional regime. This is not an arbitrary parameter slice or finite table lookup; it holds for all fixed degrees >=2 and all evaluation sequences.
